prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "EQUINIX INC" (ticker EQIX), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "EQIX", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Equinix, Inc.
markets: Managed infrastructure and bare metal services
AI inference and private AI infrastructure

mission.statement: Our mission is simple — to help you accelerate innovation.
mission.plain: Equinix wants to give companies the buildings, power and connections they need to launch new digital products faster.

about.plain: Equinix owns and runs more than 280 big, super-secure buildings around the world that are full of other companies' computers. It rents out space, power and cooling in those buildings. Inside, it plugs customers' computers directly into each other, into internet networks and into clouds like Amazon and Microsoft with private cables. Because so many networks meet in its buildings, they work like busy digital train stations.
about.customers: More than 10,500 businesses, including banks, telecom carriers, cloud providers like AWS, Microsoft and Google, AI model companies and large corporations.
about.everyday: When you stream a show, pay by card or chat with an AI app, the data often passes through an Equinix building where networks and clouds swap traffic.

money.plain: Cabinets, power and cooling for customers' servers (colocation)
Cables and virtual links that connect customers to each other and to clouds
Installation work and one-time xScale fees
Running and managing customers' IT equipment for them

money.part: xScale hyperscale and AI data centers
money.plain: Giant data center campuses for cloud and AI giants, built in joint ventures with plans to deploy $15 billion in the US

money.part: Fabric Cloud Router and AI networking
money.plain: Software networking that routes AI and cloud traffic, with bookings up 170% a year in Q2 2026

result.summary: Equinix has a strong moat built on network effects: more than 500,000 interconnections inside its buildings, which it says exceed the combined total of its next 10 competitors, make each site more valuable to the next tenant. Customers rarely move because their equipment and hundreds of cross-connects are wired in, so churn stays around 2% of recurring revenue a quarter. The weak spots are heavy capital needs, high debt and well-funded private rivals in hyperscale data centers.

pricingPower.evidence: Management reported 'firm pricing' in Q2 2026 while MRR grew 11% and churn fell to 1.8%, below its usual 2-2.5% range; gross margin rose from 48.4% in 2023 to 51.1% in 2025 and adjusted EBITDA margin reached a record 53% in Q2 2026.

moats.evidence: Equinix is the best-known name among IT buyers for neutral colocation and appears on Fortune's Most Admired list, but ordinary consumers do not know the brand.
Moving live servers and dozens of cross-connects risks outages, so quarterly MRR churn stays near 2-2.5% and was 1.8% in Q2 2026; more than 60% of existing customers added new services in 2025.

Over 500,000 interconnections (522K on its website) across about 280 data centers mean every new network, cloud or AI provider makes a site more valuable; 8 of the top 10 AI model providers run key networking workloads on Equinix.

With $9.2 billion of 2025 revenue across six continents it buys power and equipment at scale, but building costs are similar for well-financed rivals like Digital Realty, NTT and Blackstone-backed QTS.

Key interconnection hubs such as Ashburn, London, Frankfurt, Singapore and Tokyo have limited space and power, and once networks cluster in Equinix sites a new entrant cannot easily replicate that density.
Its neutral, multi-cloud position lets it partner with AWS, Microsoft and Google rather than compete, but this is not a model incumbents cannot copy.
Decades of running highly reliable sites and its software layer (Equinix Fabric, Fabric Cloud Router) give operational know-how, though data center operation is a known craft.
It controls about 3 GW of land and power with roughly 700 MW under construction in grid-constrained metros, where new power hookups can take years.

customers.evidence: Quarterly MRR churn of 1.8% in Q2 2026 (typical 2-2.5%) and more than 60% of existing customers buying new services in 2025 show high loyalty; Salesforce expanded its use of Fabric Cloud Router to 14 countries.

talent.evidence: About 14,000 employees; TrueUp shows 69% of reviewers would recommend working there and 63% approve of the CEO, decent but not top-tier, and Equinix is on Fortune's Most Admired list for 2025 and 2026.

product.evidence: It runs the world's largest retail colocation and interconnection platform (about 280 data centers, over 500,000 interconnections) and its Fabric software lets customers connect to clouds in minutes, an ecosystem rivals have not matched.

competitors.name: Digital Realty Trust
competitors.note: Largest global rival in colocation, interconnection (ServiceFabric) and hyperscale wholesale data centers

competitors.name: NTT Global Data Centers (NTT)
competitors.note: Third-largest global colocation provider, strong in Japan, India, Europe and the US

competitors.name: American Tower (CoreSite)
competitors.note: CoreSite runs interconnection-rich US retail data centers in key metros

competitors.name: Iron Mountain Data Centers
competitors.note: Fast-growing data center segment ($803M revenue in 2025) in retail and hyperscale colocation

competitors.name: KDDI (Telehouse)
competitors.note: Telehouse interconnection hubs in London, Tokyo, Paris and New York

competitors.name: GDS Holdings
competitors.note: Leading data center operator in China; its former international arm DayOne competes in Southeast Asia

competitors.name: QTS Data Centers (Blackstone)
competitors.note: Large US hyperscale and enterprise campuses competing with xScale

competitors.name: Vantage Data Centers
competitors.note: Private hyperscale campus developer in North America, EMEA and APAC

competitors.name: CyrusOne (KKR and GIP)
competitors.note: Private hyperscale and enterprise colocation in the US and Europe

competitors.name: Global Switch
competitors.note: Carrier-neutral data centers in London, Amsterdam, Singapore, Hong Kong and Sydney

competitors.name: DataBank
competitors.note: Private US edge and enterprise colocation in many secondary metros

competitors.name: Cologix
competitors.note: Private network-neutral interconnection hubs in North America

competitors.name: Switch
competitors.note: Private (DigitalBridge/IFM) large US campuses for enterprise and AI

competitors.name: Amazon Web Services
competitors.note: Public cloud substitutes for enterprise colocation, although AWS is also a big Equinix customer and partner

competitors.name: Megaport
competitors.note: Software-defined network fabric competing with Equinix Fabric for cloud connectivity

rows.name: Equinix, Digital Realty and NTT combined

threats: Hyperscalers building more of their own data centers or using rivals such as QTS, Vantage and CyrusOne for AI campuses
Power and grid limits in key metros delaying new capacity
High capital spending ($5-7 billion a year planned through 2029) and about $22 billion of debt and finance leases that raise funding costs if rates rise
Well-funded private-equity rivals (Blackstone, KKR, DigitalBridge) bidding up land, power and prices
Interconnection moving into software fabrics from Megaport or the clouds themselves, weakening the physical cross-connect advantage

Lingering reputational and legal risk from Hindenburg's March 2024 short report on AFFO accounting; the SEC closed its probe without action in November 2025, but the outcome of a US Attorney subpoena has not been reported

ceo.name: Adaire Fox-Martin
ceo.background: Trinity College Dublin graduate; former President of Go-to-Market at Google Cloud and head of Google Ireland, SAP executive board member, earlier Oracle executive; Equinix director since 2020

c1.evidence: Equinix is the largest retail colocation and interconnection provider with over 500,000 interconnections, in a data center market growing with AI and cloud; revenue grew 16% in Q2 2026.

c2.evidence: Customers choose it for the density of networks, clouds and partners inside its 280+ data centers, an ecosystem built since the company's 1998 founding that rivals cannot easily copy.

c3.evidence: Equinix is the default leader among IT buyers for interconnection, but ordinary people rarely recognize the name.

c4.evidence: Its stated mission 'to help you accelerate innovation' is generic, though management stresses its role as the digital infrastructure behind AI and cloud; the world would notice 10 more years of this work.

c6.evidence: “data centers, interconnection, reliable, digital infrastructure”: among IT and investor audiences the impression is mostly positive, while most consumers have no impression at all.

c7.evidence: Data center demand is riding cloud and AI secular trends; Equinix's 2025 bookings rose 27% to $1.6 billion and about 60% of its largest Q4 2025 deals were AI-driven.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into hyperscale AI campuses through xScale ($15 billion US JV plan), AI inference sites and software networking like Fabric Cloud Router and Fabric Geo Zones.

m1.evidence: Fox-Martin has set out a clear AI-era view (private AI, sovereign AI, AI factories and latency-sensitive inference) and a 2027-2029 plan of 10-13% annual revenue growth, but this is more strategic execution than a radical vision.

m2.evidence: She is a hired professional CEO since 2024, after careers at Google Cloud, SAP and Oracle, not a founder.

m4.evidence: She comes from customer-facing go-to-market leadership, but TrueUp shows only 63% CEO approval among employee reviewers.

m5.evidence: Equinix has a long-standing service-focused culture and keeps adding software products (Fabric, Fabric Cloud Router), but it is not known as a strong product inventor.

m6.evidence: Her background is in sales and go-to-market at Oracle, SAP and Google Cloud, not engineering.

m7.evidence: Equinix publishes sustainability and climate commitments and has no known character concerns about the CEO, but her stewardship is aimed mainly at shareholders and customers rather than a broader humanitarian cause.

m7b.evidence: No record was found of Adaire Fox-Martin giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: She keeps a polished, conventional corporate profile without a celebrity-style persona.

m9.evidence: Since 2024 bookings and margins have improved (record 53% adjusted EBITDA margin and 18% AFFO per share growth in Q2 2026, guidance raised twice in 2026), but her tenure is only about two years.

m10.evidence: Equinix is not known for frugality; it spends heavily on capacity ($4.3 billion of PP&E purchases in 2025).

c10.evidence: Its buildings indirectly support banking, streaming, cloud and AI services used by billions, but it serves businesses rather than directly improving consumers' lives.

p2.evidence: Running hundreds of always-on, power-hungry data centers with hundreds of thousands of live connections is very hard and underpins the internet and AI economy.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $5,999M in 2020 to $6,636M, $7,263M, $8,188M, $8,748M and $9,217M in 2025.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 48.8% in 2020 to 51.1% in 2025 and operating margin from 17.6% to 20.1%, but operating margin dipped to 15.2% in 2024.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 it had about $22.0 billion of debt and finance leases against $2.2 billion of cash and short-term investments (net leverage 3.6x), though equity is positive at $14.4 billion.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow rose every year from $2,310M in 2020 to $3,911M in 2025, and operating income from $1,053M to $1,848M, with one dip in 2024 ($1,328M).

v1.evidence: For a company that needs to connect to many clouds and partners in one place, Equinix offers the most interconnection points worldwide, which it says exceed its next 10 competitors combined.

v2.evidence: Equinix is on Fortune's Most Admired list for 2025 and 2026, but employee recommendation of 69% on TrueUp is only average-plus and it rarely appears in top best-employer rankings.

c5.evidence: If Equinix vanished, banks, cloud providers, streaming services and AI companies would lose the hubs where their networks meet, causing widespread internet and payment disruptions.
